stories.headline: US strikes Iran's Qeshm Island; oil prices rise amid conflict fears
stories.summary: The United States carried out strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island, with US officials describing them as limited and defensive, according to CBS via BBC. Explosions were reported on the island amid fears of renewed war. The strikes occurred ahead of US midterm elections, drawing attention to domestic political timing. Oil prices edged up about 0.5% in early Asian trading as markets weighed possible disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz. A US official told AP that US strikes hit Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz, according to PBS.
stories.whyItMatters: Relevant to GS-II International Relations: US-Iran tensions, use of force, UNSC dynamics, and GS-III energy security—oil price shocks affect India's inflation, CAD and crude imports.

static.topic: UN & Multilateral Reform
static.whatIsIt: The UN (1945) has six principal organs; the Security Council has five permanent veto-wielding members (P5) and ten elected members. India has long sought permanent UNSC membership.
static.background: India is a founding UN member and one of the largest troop contributors to peacekeeping. The G4 (India, Brazil, Germany, Japan) campaigns for expansion. Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) on Security Council reform remain inconclusive.
static.whyInNews: US strikes on Iran raise questions about use of force, UN Charter compliance and Security Council authorisation.
static.wayForward: Strengthen multilateral mechanisms, respect UN Charter, and advance India's push for UNSC reform.

static.background: US-Iran tensions have persisted since 1979. The JCPOA was signed in 2015; the US withdrew in 2018 and reimposed sanctions. Periodic tanker incidents and military posturing have kept the region volatile.
static.geography: Strait of Hormuz connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and is a critical global oil transit route. Qeshm Island sits in the Strait of Hormuz.
static.socioEconomic: India imports a significant share of its crude oil from West Asia; price spikes can affect inflation, current account deficit and energy security.
static.whyInNews: US strikes on Qeshm Island and reports of targets in the Strait of Hormuz pushed oil prices up amid fears of supply disruptions.
static.wayForward: Diplomatic de-escalation, diversification of energy sources, strategic petroleum reserves, and robust maritime security cooperation.

stories.headline: US midterms: Democrats favoured; Indian-American candidates in focus
stories.summary: US voters are voting in midterm elections that will determine control of Congress, with analyst forecasts giving Democrats an 82% chance of taking the Senate and making them strong favourites for the House. A survey shows Indian-American citizens swinging back to Democrats, with 62% intending to vote Democratic and 19% Republican, after Trump's 2024 gains faded. Several Indian-origin Democratic lawmakers—Ro Khanna, Pramila Jayapal, Ami Bera and Suhas Subramanyam—are seeking re-election. On the eve of voting, the US Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration's request to stop California from counting disputed ballots, while California's Proposition 40 proposes a one-time 5% tax on billionaires' wealth above $1 billion, mostly for healthcare. Markets saw gold ease ahead of the vote, and commentary from ORF and The Conversation highlights the election's implications for Trump's influence and for countries such as New Zealand.
stories.whyItMatters: For UPSC, US midterms illustrate comparative federalism, separation of powers, judicial review, diaspora politics and global economic spillovers—useful for GS-II IR and GS-III economy.

static.topic: US Midterms and Control of Congress: Comparative Legislative Process
static.whatIsIt: US midterm elections decide all House seats and a third of Senate seats, determining which party controls Congress and thus the legislative agenda. In India, Parliament consists of the President, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha under Article 79.
static.background: US midterms occur midway through a president's four-year term. In India, the card notes Money Bills originate only in Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha can delay but not amend money provisions, ordinances under Article 123, and standing committees scrutinise Bills.
static.socioEconomic: Control of Congress affects budget, taxation, healthcare and federal spending; diaspora voters and Indian-origin candidates feature in this election.
static.whyInNews: Democrats are favoured to gain Congress; Indian-American candidates and voters are in focus.
static.wayForward: For India, track US legislative shifts on trade, immigration, technology and defence; strengthen parliamentary committee scrutiny at home.
prelimsPointers: US midterms: all 435 House seats and about one-third of 100 Senate seats are contested.
In India, Money Bills originate only in Lok Sabha under Article 110.
static.mainsAngle: Compare legislative scrutiny and executive-legislature relations in India and the US; examine how midterm outcomes shape foreign policy.

static.whyInNews: The US Supreme Court rejected Trump's request to stop California counting disputed votes on the eve of midterms.
static.wayForward: Election disputes should be resolved swiftly and transparently; comparative study of judicial independence and election adjudication is useful.

stories.headline: Cyclone Murasu batters Andhra coast; relief and power restoration begin
stories.summary: Cyclone Murasu made landfall along the Andhra Pradesh coast on November 3, 2026, as a severe cyclonic storm, the second such system in a week. Its eye crossed the coast with wind speeds reaching up to 120 kmph, before it was expected to weaken into a deep depression by Tuesday midnight with speeds up to 75 kmph. Heavy rainfall and strong winds battered Bapatla, Prakasam and Krishna districts, uprooting trees, damaging homes and inundating crops. Transport was disrupted, with several trains and flights to and from Vijayawada cancelled, while the IMD flagged Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu as the worst-hit states. Relief operations and power restoration have begun, with Karnataka deploying 500 trained workers to assist cyclone-hit Andhra Pradesh.
stories.whyItMatters: Useful for GS-I geography (tropical cyclones), GS-III disaster management and GS-II federalism; links to climate adaptation and inter-state relief cooperation.

static.topic: Indian Monsoon & Physical Geography
static.whatIsIt: The Indian monsoon is a seasonal reversal of winds driven by differential heating, the ITCZ shift and the Tibetan Plateau's heat pump; it delivers about 75% of annual rainfall during June–September.
static.background: El Niño usually weakens the monsoon, La Niña strengthens it, and the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) also modulates it. The Western Ghats and Himalayan rivers define drainage; peninsular rivers are rain-fed. Tropical cyclones are a key term in this physical geography framework.
static.geography: Bay of Bengal and the Andhra Pradesh coast, including Bapatla, Prakasam and Krishna districts, are exposed to cyclonic systems.
static.socioEconomic: Cyclones bring heavy rain, strong winds, crop inundation, power outages and transport disruption, requiring disaster preparedness and relief.
static.whyInNews: Cyclone Murasu made landfall along the Andhra Pradesh coast, bringing heavy rain and winds up to 120 kmph before weakening into a deep depression.
static.wayForward: Strengthen early warning, cyclone shelters, mangrove buffers and climate-resilient coastal infrastructure; integrate monsoon variability and cyclone risk into disaster preparedness.
prelimsPointers: The Indian monsoon delivers about 75% of annual rainfall during June–September.
El Niño usually weakens the monsoon; La Niña strengthens it; the IOD also modulates it.
Himalayan rivers are perennial (snow-fed); peninsular rivers are seasonal.
static.mainsAngle: Monsoon variability and climate change; disaster preparedness for floods and cyclones.

static.topic: Federalism & Centre-State Relations
static.whatIsIt: India is a quasi-federal union: powers are divided between the Union and States via the Union, State and Concurrent Lists (Seventh Schedule), with residuary powers with the Union (Art. 248).
static.background: Sarkaria (1983) and Punchhi (2007) Commissions examined Centre-State balance. The Governor (Art. 153) is the Centre's constitutional representative and a flashpoint over assent to Bills (Art. 200) and reservation of Bills for the President (Art. 201).
static.geography: Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka are neighbouring southern states; inter-state resource deployment for disaster relief is a practical example of regional cooperation.
static.socioEconomic: Post-cyclone power restoration and relief require trained manpower, coordination and fiscal support, illustrating cooperative federalism in disaster response.
static.whyInNews: Karnataka is deploying 500 trained workers to restore power in cyclone-hit Andhra Pradesh, showing inter-state cooperation during a disaster.
static.wayForward: Institutionalise inter-state disaster resource sharing, joint training and rapid response protocols under cooperative federalism.
prelimsPointers: Concurrent List: union law prevails on repugnancy unless state law reserved for President's assent (Art. 254).
Inter-State Council (Art. 263) is a recommendatory dispute-resolution body.
static.mainsAngle: Recent spats over Governor's assent and fiscal devolution — assess cooperative federalism in practice.

static.topic: Agriculture, MSP & Food Security
static.whatIsIt: Minimum Support Price (MSP) is announced by the government (CACP recommendations) for 22 mandated crops. Food security is backed by the National Food Security Act, 2013, and the PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana grain distribution.
static.background: Green Revolution (1960s) made India food-sufficient. Shanta Kumar Committee (2015) reviewed FCI operations. PM-KISAN gives ₹6,000/year income support. The three 2020 farm laws were repealed in 2021.
static.geography: Coastal Andhra Pradesh, including Bapatla, Prakasam and Krishna districts, is an agricultural region vulnerable to cyclone-related crop inundation.
static.socioEconomic: Crop damage affects farmer incomes, local food supply and rural livelihoods; relief, compensation and crop insurance become critical after cyclones.
static.whyInNews: Cyclone Murasu inundated crops in parts of coastal Andhra Pradesh, raising concerns for agricultural recovery and food security.
static.wayForward: Strengthen crop insurance, timely compensation, climate-resilient seed varieties and post-disaster agricultural extension.
prelimsPointers: MSP is a price assurance, not a legal right; procurement is concentrated in wheat/paddy.
NFSA covers up to 75% rural and 50% urban population.
static.mainsAngle: Reforming MSP and procurement while raising farmer incomes; water-fertiliser sustainability.

stories.headline: SC allows green crackers; Delhi AQI worsens amid Diwali pollution row
stories.summary: The Supreme Court permitted the bursting of certified green firecrackers in Delhi-NCR on November 7 and 8, with specified windows of 6–7 am and 8–10 pm, while hearing the larger issue of a year-round firecracker ban. In its remarks, the Court observed that a blanket prohibition 'seems ideal' but noted insufficient data to conclude that such bans alone solve air pollution. Separately, Delhi's air quality deteriorated sharply, with AQI rising from 117 on Saturday to 261 on Sunday and 324 by Monday afternoon—the season's first 'very poor' reading. In Mumbai, the Bombay High Court expressed displeasure over the BMC's removal of actor Dia Mirza's eco-friendly Diwali video and directed the civic body to re-upload it, after a political row over the campaign.
stories.whyItMatters: Tests the judiciary's role in environmental regulation versus cultural practices, and highlights the need for evidence-based, regional air quality governance—key themes for GS-II polity and GS-III environment.

static.background: The Air Act, 1981 created pollution control boards. The CPCB sets national ambient air quality standards. GRAP is an emergency response mechanism for Delhi-NCR. The CAQM Act, 2021 established a statutory commission for air quality management in the NCR and adjoining areas.

static.wayForward: Adopt source-apportionment-based action, regional airshed management, cleaner fuels, public transport expansion, strict enforcement and public awareness.

stories.headline: Russia strikes Kherson aid site, killing 26; Europe rehearses post-peace deployment
stories.summary: Russian strikes hit a village in Ukraine's southern Kherson region, killing at least 26 people at a facility described in reports as an aid centre and, in one account, a school. Kyiv said the attack came after the collapse of a local ceasefire — described as the longest truce in the war since Russia's 2022 invasion — and reported that around nine heavy 3,000 kg aerial bombs were used. Ukrainian officials called the strike 'utterly horrific', and the timing undercut expectations of movement toward a negotiated settlement. Separately, Western officials said thousands of European troops will rehearse a future deployment to Ukraine in the event of peace, stressing that such a force would not take part in offensive operations. The United States simultaneously announced a fresh round of peace talks, keeping a diplomatic track alive even as fighting continues.
stories.whyItMatters: The strike and the European deployment rehearsal together test the two pillars of the Ukraine question — the credibility of ceasefires and humanitarian protection, and the shape of post-conflict security guarantees. For UPSC, it feeds directly into questions on UNSC paralysis, peace support operations and India's strategic balancing.

static.topic: UN Security Council and the Russia–Ukraine War

static.whatIsIt: The UN Security Council is the UN's principal organ for international peace and security, with 15 members — five permanent veto-wielding members (China, France, Russia, UK, US) and ten elected members serving two-year terms. static.background: The UN was founded in 1945; India is a founding member and among the largest troop contributors to UN peacekeeping. static.topic: Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) Scheme and Citizenship Law
static.whatIsIt: OCI is a long-term visa/immigration status for foreign nationals of Indian origin, created under Section 7A of the Citizenship Act, 1955. It is not dual citizenship: an OCI cardholder remains a foreign national and does not hold Indian citizenship.
static.background: Part II (Articles 5–11) of the Constitution deals with citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution; the Citizenship Act, 1955 governs acquisition and termination of citizenship by birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory. The OCI scheme was introduced through the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2003 and operationalised thereafter, replacing the earlier PIO card scheme, which was merged into OCI in 2015. Section 7D empowers the Central Government to cancel OCI registration on grounds such as obtaining it by fraud, a sentence of imprisonment of two years or more within five years of registration, or action in the interest of the sovereignty and security of India.
static.socioEconomic: OCI is a key instrument of India's diaspora engagement, easing travel, property holding and business for persons of Indian origin abroad, while stopping short of any political or electoral role.
static.whyInNews: The Bombay High Court observed that OCI cardholders are not citizens while asking actor Imran Khan to apologise for participating in a protest against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls; his stay in India was subsequently extended.
static.wayForward: Clarify through executive guidelines and judicial precedent the permissible scope of political expression for foreign nationals and OCI cardholders, distinguishing peaceful protest from electoral or political activity barred to non-citizens.
prelimsPointers: OCI cardholders cannot vote, contest elections, hold constitutional posts (President, Vice-President, judge of the Supreme Court or a High Court) or take up government employment.
OCI is not dual citizenship — the Constitution provides for single citizenship; OCI is a long-term visa status with limited rights.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss whether the OCI scheme adequately balances diaspora outreach with the constitutional principle of single citizenship, and examine the grounds and procedural safeguards for cancellation of OCI registration.

static.topic: High Courts, Judicial Review and Writ Jurisdiction

Judicial review is the power to test legislative and executive action against the Constitution.
static.background: The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998). Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine. PILs expanded access to justice from the late 1970s. Article 32 (Supreme Court) and Article 226 (High Courts) provide writ jurisdiction.
static.whyInNews: The Bombay High Court exercised its jurisdiction to condition the actor's continued stay in India on an apology, illustrating how constitutional courts regulate the conduct of foreign nationals within their territorial jurisdiction.

static.mainsAngle: Examine judicial backlog, vacancies and pendency, and the balance between judicial independence and accountability.

static.topic: Electoral Rolls and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR)
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Elections; Election Commission of India; Representation of the People Act, 1950
static.whatIsIt: SIR is a more intensive, door-to-door verification of existing electoral-roll entries, as distinct from the routine annual revision of rolls. It is conducted by the Election Commission of India.
static.background: The ECI superintends elections under Article 324. Preparation and revision of electoral rolls is governed by the Representation of the People Act, 1950 (Sections 21–23) and the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960. In the SIR mode, enumerators verify existing entries afresh and propose deletion of dead, shifted or duplicate entries, with notice and an opportunity of hearing before removal.
static.socioEconomic: Roll revision directly affects access to political representation and, indirectly, welfare targeting; large-scale deletions raise concerns about disenfranchisement of marginalised and migrant voters.
static.whyInNews: Protests against SIR — in which the actor participated — led the Bombay High Court to seek an apology, while an editorial argued the protests reflect a fear that the process could subvert popular will.
static.wayForward: Strengthen procedural safeguards — reasoned individual notice before deletion, accessible appeal mechanisms and independent audit — to preserve both roll integrity and the right to vote.
prelimsPointers: The ECI is a constitutional body under Article 324; electoral rolls are prepared and revised under the Representation of the People Act, 1950.
Deletion from the rolls requires notice and an opportunity of hearing, with appeals lying to the District Election Officer and the Chief Electoral Officer.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate whether intensive roll-revision exercises strengthen electoral integrity or risk disenfranchisement, and suggest safeguards consistent with the constitutional right to vote.

static.syllabusNode: Internal Security — maritime security; piracy and armed robbery at sea; security of sea lanes of communication
static.whatIsIt: Maritime security covers the protection of shipping, ports, offshore assets and sea lanes from piracy, armed robbery, terrorism, smuggling and state-sponsored harassment. For India, the western Indian Ocean — Arabian Sea, Gulf of Oman, Gulf of Aden, Bab-el-Mandeb and the Red Sea — forms the critical corridor for energy and trade.
static.background: Piracy off Somalia surged from around 2008, prompting the Indian Navy to begin anti-piracy escort operations in the Gulf of Aden from October 2008. Following attacks on tankers in the Gulf of Oman in mid-2019, India launched Operation Sankalp in June 2019 to escort Indian-flagged vessels through the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman. Multilateral frameworks include the Djibouti Code of Conduct (2009) for western Indian Ocean and Gulf of Aden states, the Contact Group on Piracy off the Coast of Somalia, the Combined Maritime Forces (including CTF-150 and CTF-151), and EUNAVFOR's Operation Atalanta. India also hosts the Information Fusion Centre – Indian Ocean Region (IFC-IOR) at Gurugram, set up in 2018, for maritime domain awareness.
static.geography: The Gulf of Oman links the Arabian Sea to the Strait of Hormuz, the world's most important oil chokepoint, and lies between Iran to the north and Oman and the UAE to the south. The wider western Indian Ocean corridor includes the Gulf of Aden, Bab-el-Mandeb and the Red Sea.
static.socioEconomic: A very large share of India's external trade by volume moves by sea, and India is among the largest suppliers of seafarers to global shipping. Disruption or attacks in the Gulf corridor raise insurance costs, freight rates and energy import risk, and directly endanger Indian livelihoods at sea.
static.whyInNews: An attack on the MSV AL JUSUFI near Oman killed one Indian national and led to the rescue of 13 of the 14 Indians on board.
static.wayForward: Sustained naval presence and escort operations, expanded maritime domain awareness through IFC-IOR and coastal radar chains, stronger coordination with littoral states and the Combined Maritime Forces, and clearer standard operating procedures for crew safety and consular response.
prelimsPointers: MSV stands for Motor Sailing Vessel, a dhow-type craft widely used in Gulf and Arabian Sea trade.
The Gulf of Oman connects the Arabian Sea with the Strait of Hormuz.
Operation Sankalp was launched by the Indian Navy in June 2019 for maritime security in the Gulf of Oman and Persian Gulf.
IFC-IOR, India's maritime information fusion centre, is located at Gurugram.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how attacks on commercial shipping in the western Indian Ocean affect India's energy security, trade and seafarer safety, and evaluate the adequacy of India's current maritime security architecture.

static.topic: India's maritime security operations and anti-piracy deployments
static.syllabusNode: Internal Security — role of the armed forces in safeguarding national interests; Indian Navy deployments
static.whatIsIt: The Indian Navy undertakes anti-piracy patrols, convoy escort, surveillance and humanitarian assistance missions in the Indian Ocean Region, often in coordination with multilateral naval task forces.
static.background: Anti-piracy escort missions in the Gulf of Aden began in 2008. Operation Sankalp followed in June 2019 for the Gulf of Oman and Persian Gulf. India participates in multilateral exercises such as Milan, hosts IFC-IOR, and cooperates with partners including the Combined Maritime Forces and regional navies on information sharing and escort coordination.
static.geography: Deployments span the Gulf of Aden, Gulf of Oman, Persian Gulf, Arabian Sea and, more recently, the wider western Indian Ocean including the Red Sea approaches.
static.socioEconomic: Naval deployments protect trade routes worth a substantial share of India's GDP-linked external commerce and support the safety of Indian seafarers and fishermen.
static.whyInNews: The attack near Oman highlights the continuing threat to small commercial vessels and the role of naval and consular response mechanisms.
static.wayForward: Strengthen persistent surveillance, integrate unmanned and aerial maritime domain awareness assets, deepen regional information-sharing agreements, and institutionalise rapid consular and rescue coordination for Indian crews.
prelimsPointers: Operation Sankalp is the Indian Navy's maritime security operation in the Gulf of Oman and Persian Gulf, begun in June 2019.
India's anti-piracy escort role in the Gulf of Aden dates to 2008.
IFC-IOR was established in 2018 to enhance maritime domain awareness in the Indian Ocean Region.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the evolution of the Indian Navy's anti-piracy and maritime security operations and assess whether India needs a more permanent presence in the western Indian Ocean.

static.topic: Safety and welfare of Indian workers and seafarers abroad
static.syllabusNode: Government policies and interventions; India and its diaspora; consular services and welfare of Indians abroad
static.whatIsIt: India's consular and diaspora welfare framework covers evacuation, legal aid, financial assistance and grievance redressal for Indians abroad, including seafarers on foreign-flagged and Indian vessels.
static.background: The Ministry of External Affairs runs a consular, passport and visa division supported by missions abroad. Key instruments include the Indian Community Welfare Fund (ICWF) for distressed Indians abroad, the e-Migrate system for regulating emigration of workers, and the MADAD portal for consular grievances. Large-scale evacuations such as those from the Gulf and other conflict zones have shaped this machinery over time.
static.geography: The Gulf and West Asia host a very large Indian expatriate population, making the region central to consular operations.
static.socioEconomic: Remittances from the Gulf form a significant component of India's remittance inflows, and seafaring is an important source of employment for Indian coastal communities.
static.whyInNews: One Indian national was killed and 13 rescued after an attack on a vessel near Oman, requiring consular and rescue coordination.
static.wayForward: Faster distress-response protocols with shipowners and flag states, stronger pre-departure orientation for seafarers, expanded ICWF coverage, and real-time tracking of Indian crew on vulnerable routes.
prelimsPointers: The Indian Community Welfare Fund provides emergency assistance to distressed Indians abroad.
MADAD is the MEA's online consular grievance redressal portal.
e-Migrate is the online system for regulating emigration of Indian workers.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate the effectiveness of India's consular and diaspora welfare mechanisms in responding to emergencies involving Indian workers and seafarers abroad.

stories.headline: Sri Lanka's organised crime bill faces 20 Supreme Court petitions
stories.summary: Sri Lanka's Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill has drawn 20 petitions in the Supreme Court challenging its constitutionality, Deputy Speaker Rizvi Salih informed Parliament. The petitions were filed under Article 121(1) of Sri Lanka's Constitution, the provision that allows pre-enactment scrutiny of a Bill's constitutional validity, and copies have reached the Speaker. The development places the legislation's passage in doubt until the apex court rules on whether its provisions are consistent with the Constitution. The Bill has been politically contentious, and the volume of challenges signals broad opposition from rights groups, lawyers and political actors. The matter now sits at the intersection of legislative intent and judicial review in Sri Lanka's constitutional scheme.
stories.whyItMatters: Illustrates pre-enactment judicial review — a model distinct from India's largely post-enactment review — and is useful for comparative constitutionalism and India's neighbourhood diplomacy questions.

perspectives.take: Wire-based (PTI) institutional reporting that frames the story procedurally — the Deputy Speaker's statement in Parliament and the Article 121(1) route — rather than taking a position on the Bill's merits.

static.topic: Judicial Review and Pre-Enactment Constitutional Scrutiny
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary: Supreme Court, High Courts & Judicial Review
static.whatIsIt: Judicial review is the power of a constitutional court to test legislation against the Constitution. Sri Lanka's Article 121(1) permits challenges to a Bill before it becomes law, so the Supreme Court can rule on constitutionality at the drafting stage itself.
static.background: India's Supreme Court (Art. 124) is the apex court and guardian of the Constitution; High Courts (Art. 214) exercise parallel jurisdiction. The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998), and Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine. PILs expanded access to justice from the late 1970s, with writ jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 226.
static.whyInNews: Twenty petitions were filed in Sri Lanka's Supreme Court under Article 121(1) against the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill, triggering pre-enactment judicial review.
static.wayForward: Compare pre-enactment and post-enactment review models; assess whether early judicial scrutiny improves legislative quality or delays urgent law-and-order legislation.
prelimsPointers: India's writ jurisdiction: Article 32 (Supreme Court) and Article 226 (High Courts).
Original jurisdiction over Centre–state disputes lies with the Supreme Court under Article 131; advisory jurisdiction under Article 143.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how pre-enactment judicial review differs from India's post-enactment model, and evaluate its implications for legislative supremacy and fundamental rights.

static.topic: Legislative Process and Parliamentary Scrutiny of Bills
static.whatIsIt: Parliament (Article 79) comprises the President, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha; a Bill becomes law after passage by both Houses and Presidential assent (Article 111). Departmentally Related Standing Committees scrutinise Bills before passage.
static.background: Money Bills (Art. 110) originate only in the Lok Sabha, where the Rajya Sabha may delay but not amend money provisions. Ordinances (Art. 123) may be promulgated when Parliament is not in session and must be approved within six weeks of reassembly.
static.whyInNews: The challenge to Sri Lanka's Bill was disclosed on the floor of Parliament by the Deputy Speaker, highlighting the legislature–judiciary interface during law-making.
static.wayForward: Strengthen committee referral and pre-legislative consultation so that constitutional objections are addressed before enactment rather than litigated after.
prelimsPointers: A no-confidence motion can be moved only in the Lok Sabha.
A Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha lapses on dissolution of the Lok Sabha only if it has not yet been passed by the Lok Sabha.
static.mainsAngle: Assess declining legislative scrutiny and falling committee referrals; treat parliamentary productivity as a governance indicator.

static.topic: India–Sri Lanka Relations and Neighbourhood Diplomacy
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and its Neighbourhood
static.whatIsIt: India and Sri Lanka share a maritime boundary and a dense web of political, economic and cultural ties, managed through India's Neighbourhood First policy and its SAGAR vision for the Indian Ocean.
static.background: The 1987 Indo–Sri Lanka Accord framed India's engagement on the ethnic question. The India–Sri Lanka Free Trade Agreement (signed 1998, in force 2000) deepened economic ties, with an Economic and Technology Cooperation Agreement (ETCA) under discussion. Recurring irritants include the fishermen issue, Katchatheevu, and periodic concerns over third-country presence in Sri Lankan projects.
static.geography: Sri Lanka is a teardrop-shaped island in the Indian Ocean, separated from India by the Palk Strait and Gulf of Mannar; Colombo is its commercial capital and Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte the legislative capital.
static.socioEconomic: Sri Lanka's economy depends heavily on tourism, remittances, tea and apparel exports, making it sensitive to political instability and external shocks.
static.whyInNews: Constitutional litigation over a major crime law in Colombo is relevant to India because political and legal stability in Sri Lanka directly affects regional security and Indian Ocean connectivity projects.
static.wayForward: Track Sri Lanka's domestic legal and political trajectory closely while advancing connectivity, energy and people-to-people ties under Neighbourhood First.
prelimsPointers: Sri Lanka's Parliament is unicameral, with 225 members.
Sri Lanka's legislative capital is Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte; Colombo is the commercial capital.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how domestic political and constitutional developments in Sri Lanka shape India's neighbourhood policy and Indian Ocean strategy.

prelims: Sri Lanka's Constitution provides for pre-enactment judicial review: petitions under Article 121(1) challenge a Bill's constitutionality before it becomes law.
The Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill has attracted 20 such petitions, as disclosed in Parliament by Deputy Speaker Rizvi Salih.
Sri Lanka's Parliament is unicameral with 225 members; the Speaker receives copies of petitions filed under Article 121(1).
stories.mainsQuestion: Pre-enactment judicial review allows a constitutional court to test a Bill before it becomes law. Examine this model with reference to Sri Lanka's Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill, and compare it with India's predominantly post-enactment model of judicial review.

stories.headline: Goyal chairs roundtable to strengthen biopharma startups and bioeconomy growth
stories.summary: Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal chaired a roundtable focused on strengthening India's biopharma startup ecosystem and accelerating bioeconomy growth. The consultation brought the government face-to-face with industry and startup stakeholders to identify bottlenecks and growth levers in the sector. Discussions centred on scaling innovation, improving the ease of doing business for biotech ventures, and linking research output to commercial manufacturing. The exercise fits into the wider policy push to make biotechnology a pillar of India's manufacturing and export ambitions. Outcomes are expected to feed into follow-up policy and facilitation measures rather than a single standalone scheme.
stories.whyItMatters: Biopharma and the bioeconomy sit at the intersection of Science & Technology, Industry and Health policy — a recurring GS-III theme and a live example of government–industry consultation shaping industrial policy.

perspectives.take: Official government framing: presents the roundtable as a proactive ministerial outreach to energise the biopharma startup ecosystem and speed up bioeconomy growth; no dissenting or industry-critical voice is carried.

static.topic: BioE3 Policy (Biotechnology for Economy, Environment and Employment)
static.syllabusNode: Science and Technology — Biotechnology; Government Policies and Interventions
static.whatIsIt: A national policy framework approved by the Union Cabinet to promote bio-manufacturing and bio-foundry capacity, positioning biotechnology as a driver of jobs, sustainable manufacturing and a circular bioeconomy.
static.background: India's biotech policy journey moved from the National Biotechnology Development Strategy to a dedicated bio-manufacturing-oriented framework. The BioE3 Policy was cleared by the Union Cabinet in 2024, with the Department of Biotechnology as the nodal agency, and it seeks to move beyond health biotechnology into industrial, agricultural and environmental applications.
static.geography: Pan-India; bio-manufacturing clusters are concentrated around existing biotech parks and research institutions in states such as Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana, Gujarat and Himachal Pradesh.
static.socioEconomic: Aims at high-skill job creation, import substitution in biologics and enzymes, and value addition to agricultural and biomass waste streams; also relevant to rural bio-entrepreneurship.
static.whyInNews: The ministerial roundtable on biopharma startups and bioeconomy growth is a follow-through on the policy's implementation agenda.
static.wayForward: Translate policy intent into operational support — shared bio-foundry infrastructure, streamlined regulatory pathways, and sustained risk capital for early-stage biotech ventures.

static.topic: National Biopharma Mission and BIRAC
static.syllabusNode: Science and Technology — Biotechnology; Health; Industrial Policy
static.whatIsIt: The National Biopharma Mission is a DBT programme aimed at accelerating biopharmaceutical development and strengthening the ecosystem for affordable indigenous biologics; BIRAC is the DBT's public-sector enterprise that funds and incubates biotech startups.
static.background: The National Biopharma Mission was launched in 2017 with World Bank co-financing and is implemented through BIRAC. BIRAC was set up by DBT in 2012 as a not-for-profit vehicle to support innovation, early-stage funding and incubation in biotechnology.
static.geography: National in scope, delivered through BIRAC-supported incubators, biotech parks and institutional partners across states.
static.socioEconomic: Targets affordable access to vaccines, therapeutics and diagnostics; supports startup formation, IP generation and skilled employment in the biotech sector.
static.whyInNews: The roundtable specifically addressed strengthening the biopharma startup ecosystem, the core mandate of the Mission and BIRAC.
static.wayForward: Deepen late-stage and scale-up funding, ease clinical trial and approval processes, and build industry–academia linkages so that publicly funded research reaches the market.
prelimsPointers: BIRAC is a DBT set-up that funds and incubates biotech startups.
The National Biopharma Mission is implemented through BIRAC with World Bank support.
static.mainsAngle: Assess whether India's public biotech funding architecture adequately bridges the 'valley of death' between research and commercialisation.

static.topic: India's Bioeconomy and the Biotech Startup Ecosystem
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Growth, Development and Employment; Science and Technology
static.whatIsIt: The bioeconomy covers economic output derived from biotechnology and biological resources — biopharmaceuticals, bio-agriculture, bio-industrial products and bio-energy. India's biotech startup base has expanded rapidly across health, agri-tech and industrial biotech.
static.background: India's biotech sector grew from a research-and-institution-led base into a startup-driven ecosystem over the last two decades, supported by DBT programmes, BIRAC funding, state biotech policies and a large pool of scientific talent. The government has set an ambitious bioeconomy target for 2030.
static.geography: Clustered in biotech hubs such as Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, Ahmedabad and the National Capital Region, with emerging clusters in other states.
static.socioEconomic: Contributes to exports, high-value employment, affordable healthcare and sustainable alternatives to petrochemical-based products; faces constraints in patient capital, scale-up manufacturing and regulatory timelines.
static.whyInNews: The Commerce and Industry Minister's roundtable is aimed at removing bottlenecks and accelerating bioeconomy growth through the startup route.
static.wayForward: Combine fiscal incentives, regulatory simplification, dedicated bio-manufacturing parks and stronger industry–academia collaboration to convert scientific strength into global market share.
prelimsPointers: Biopharma, bio-agri and bio-industrial products are the main segments of the bioeconomy.
India's biotech startup growth is concentrated in a few states with strong research institutions and biotech parks.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the potential of the bioeconomy as an engine of India's manufacturing and export growth, and the policy support required to realise it.

stories.mainsQuestion: India's scientific talent and startup energy are well recognised, yet the bioeconomy remains under-scaled. Examine the structural constraints in India's biopharma and biotech startup ecosystem and suggest measures to convert research strength into manufacturing and export leadership.

stories.headline: SC: Inmates of matrimonial home must explain woman's unnatural death
stories.summary: The Supreme Court has held that inmates of a matrimonial home must explain the unnatural death of a woman occurring there, invoking Section 106 of the Indian Evidence Act. That section places the burden of proving a fact especially within knowledge on the person who possesses such knowledge. The Court reasoned that co-inhabitants of the matrimonial home are best placed to explain the circumstances of such a death. The ruling reinforces evidentiary expectations in cases involving unnatural deaths of women within matrimonial homes. It is expected to guide trial courts in appreciating evidence in such matters.
stories.whyItMatters: Important for GS-II judiciary and women-safety debates; tests understanding of evidence law, burden of proof and the Supreme Court's role in gender justice.

perspectives.take: Frames the ruling as a significant interpretation of Section 106 Evidence Act, emphasising that inmates of the matrimonial home must account for a woman's unnatural death; legal news outlet focused on doctrinal significance.

stories.headline: Delhi HC quashes CIC order seeking RTI data on delayed judgments
stories.summary: The Delhi High Court has set aside an order of the Central Information Commission that had directed the High Court to furnish, under the Right to Information Act, data relating to judgments delivered beyond stipulated timelines. The dispute sits at the intersection of the citizen's right to information about the functioning of public authorities and the institutional autonomy of the judiciary in its administrative and judicial work. The High Court's intervention effectively reverses the Commission's direction, restoring the earlier position in that particular proceeding. The ruling adds to the evolving jurisprudence on how far RTI obligations extend to court registries and judicial administration, an area where the Supreme Court has previously held that the office of the Chief Justice is a public authority while carving out protection for judicial decision-making.
stories.whyItMatters: Tests the balance between transparency and accountability of the judiciary on one hand and judicial independence on the other — a recurring GS-II theme on RTI, pendency and institutional autonomy.

perspectives.take: Legal-news framing that foregrounds the High Court's judicial review of the CIC's direction, treating it as a significant appellate outcome on RTI's reach into court administration.

static.topic: Right to Information Act, 2005
static.whatIsIt: A statutory regime obliging public authorities to disclose information to citizens on request, subject to defined exemptions, with an appellate mechanism headed by Information Commissions at the Central and State levels.
static.background: Rooted in the freedom-of-information movement in Rajasthan and the 1997 Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan campaign; the Freedom of Information Act, 2002 was followed by the RTI Act, 2005, which came into force on 12 October 2005. The RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019 altered the tenure and salary provisions for Information Commissioners. In 2019 the Supreme Court held that the office of the Chief Justice of India is a 'public authority' under the Act, while recognising limits where disclosure touches judicial deliberation.
static.socioEconomic: RTI is a key instrument of social audit — used for MGNREGA wage records, ration shop lists and municipal spending — and is therefore tied to welfare delivery accountability.
static.whyInNews: A CIC direction to the Delhi High Court for data on delayed judgments was quashed by the High Court, reviving debate on RTI's application to court administration.
static.wayForward: Courts can voluntarily publish case-age and disposal data under Section 4 proactive disclosure, reducing the need for contested RTI applications while preserving confidentiality of judicial deliberation.

RTI applies to 'public authorities' as defined in Section 2(h), which includes bodies established by the Constitution.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss whether transparency obligations under the RTI Act should extend to the administrative functioning of the higher judiciary, and how such disclosure can be reconciled with judicial independence.
